'''Thomas Reeve Kaiser''' (2 May 1924 – 2 July 1998)<ref name=Independent/> was an Australian physicist and geophysicist. He was awarded the [[Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society]] in 1994, and was a known [[communist]] during the [[Cold War]].

==Biography==
===Early life and education===
Born in [[Ivanhoe, Victoria]],<ref name=Deery/> Kaiser came from the working class. His father was a factory worker, and many in his family worked in the mining industry.<ref name=Martin>{{cite book |last1=Martin |first1=Brian |title=Intellectual Suppression: Australian Case Histories, Analysis and Responses |date=1986 |publisher=Angus and Robertson |location=Sydney |pages=11–23 |url=https://documents.uow.edu.au/~bmartin/pubs/86is/Buckley.html |access-date=20 September 2024}}</ref> He received his bachelor's degree in 1943 and his master's degree in 1946 from the [[University of Melbourne]]. He received his master's degree whilst working for [[CSIRO]] at the Sydney Radiophysics Laboratory,<ref name=Independent>{{cite news |last1=Alleyne |first1=Hugo |title=Obituary: Professor Tom Kaiser |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/obituary-professor-tom-kaiser-1171316.html |access-date=20 September 2024 |work=The Independent |date=13 August 1998}}</ref> having started working for CSIRO in 1944.<ref name=Deery/> During the [[Second World War]], Kaiser participated in radar research.<ref name=Deery/> In 1947, Kaiser attended [[University College, Oxford]] to study [[nuclear physics]], mostly working at the [[Clarendon Laboratory]]. He completed his Doctorate on the acceleration of charged particles in two years.<ref name=Independent/> His dissertation was entitled ''On the Capture of Particles into Synchrotron Orbits'', and he was advised by [[Frederick Lindemann]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Thomas Kaiser |url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=212093 |website=Mathematics Genealogy Project |publisher=North Dakota State University |access-date=20 September 2024}}</ref> During his time at Oxford, Kaiser helped construct the 16MeV [[Betatron]] and conducted experiments using the equipment.<ref name=Deery/>

===Early career and political activity===
Kaiser's scholarship at the University of Oxford was withdrawn in 1949 during [[McCarthyism]] due to Kaiser's communist beliefs, forcing Kaiser to return to [[Australia]] with his British wife Pamela (also a member of the Communist party), who he had married earlier that same year.<ref name=Independent/><ref name=nationalarchives>{{cite web |title=Thomas Reeve KAISER: Australian. Pamela Eileen KAISER, alias POUND: British. Thomas... |url=https://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/C11527130 |website=National Archives |publisher=UK Government |access-date=20 September 2024}}</ref> This was a result of Kaiser's participation in a demonstration outside [[Australia House]] against the Australian government's treatment of coal miners during the [[1949 Australian coal strike]], which became an incident named "the Kaiser affair".<ref name=Independent/> Following the demonstration, on 19 August 1949 Kaiser was ordered to return to Australia by [[Ian Clunies Ross]] (head of [[CSIRO]]) and was banned from research positions in nuclear or radio physics.<ref name=Martin/> Kaiser was dismissed from his paid role at [[CSIRO]] after Kaiser refused to immediately return to Australia. Kaiser departed for Australia on 24 November 1949.<ref name=Deery/> The affair received significant coverage in Australian printed media.<ref name=Guardian/>

Following his forced return to Australia, and his inability to gain employment, Kaiser engaged extensively in political work for the [[Communist Party of Australia]], being under constant surveillance.<ref name=Deery/> By 1950, Kaiser's continued political activities meant it was necessary for him to leave Australia.<ref name=Independent/> He departed for England on 30 July 1950.<ref name=Deery/> Kaiser returned to the United Kingdom to take up a post at the [[University of Manchester]], working under professor [[Patrick Blackett]]<ref name=nationalarchives/> at [[Jodrell Bank]].<ref name=Independent/> Whilst present at Jodrell bank, Kaiser became interested in the radio signal produced when [[interstellar dust]] interacts with the [[Earth's atmosphere]] and leaves ionized residue. He would go on to be an important figure in the study of [[meteor]] interactions with the upper atmosphere,<ref name=Independent/> in particular with his 1953 paper on the cross section and radio echos of meteors interacting with the upper atmosphere,<ref name=Hughes/> which has been called the definitive work on the subject.<ref name=BAS/><ref name=Times/>

In the early 1950s, Kaiser joined the [[Communist Party of Great Britain]] and remained politically active. In 1952, he sent a telegram to [[President Truman]] on behalf of [[Julius and Ethel Rosenberg]]. The telegram was addressed from Jodrell Bank, leading to [[Bernard Lovell]] being alerted of his membership of the Communist party; eventually this would lead to Kaiser leaving Jodrell Bank.<ref name=Guardian>{{cite news |last1=Jeanne |first1=Wisemann |title=TOM KAISER - METEORS AND SOCIALISM |url=https://tomkaiser.tripod.com/guardian_obit.html |access-date=20 September 2024 |work=The Guardian |date=5 August 1998}}</ref> In 1954, Kaiser was named during the [[Petrov Affair]] as a person of interest to Soviet intelligence agencies.<ref name=nationalarchives/>

In 1955, Kaiser joined the [[University of Reading]] as a senior lecturer.<ref name=Independent/> In 1956, Kaiser left the Communist party in protest at the Soviet response to the [[Hungarian Revolution of 1956]].<ref name=Guardian/>

Through the 1950s, Kaiser applied to at least 40 scientific positions in [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]], but was consistently rejected.<ref name=Deery>{{cite web |last1=Deery |first1=Phillip |title=Scientific Freedom and Post-war Politics: Australia,  1945-55 |url=https://vuir.vu.edu.au/587/1/Scientific_Freedom_and_Post-war_Politics.pdf |publisher=University of Victoria |access-date=20 September 2024}}</ref>

===Later career===
In 1956 he became a Senior Lecturer at the [[University of Sheffield]],<ref name=Independent/> and founded the Space Physics group.<ref name=BAS/> In 1966 he was appointed to the chair of space physics and in 1987 he became emeritus.<ref name=Independent/> Despite becoming less politically active, Kaiser was still restricted from entering the [[United States]] for much of his career.<ref name=BAS>{{cite web |last1=AJS |title=TOM KAISER (1924--1998) |url=http://www.nerc-bas.ac.uk/public/uasd//mist/kaiser.html |publisher=British Antarctic Survey |access-date=20 September 2024}}</ref> As late as 1972, Kaiser was still refused a visa to enter the United States to see the launch of a satellite he helped design.<ref name=Deery/> He still remained a socialist, and advocated against the [[Vietnam War]] and for [[nuclear disarmament]].<ref name=Guardian/>

Kaiser played a part in the design of equipment on board both [[Ariel 3]] and [[Ariel 4]], contributing to the [[VLF]] equipment on the satellites, and assisted in their operation from ground level.<ref name=BAS/> Kaiser was among the first to understand the potential role of [[Antarctica|Antarctic]] observations for Space Physics,<ref name=Guardian/> and participated in physics research at [[Halley Station]], mostly contributing to setting up permanent [[VLF]] receivers.<ref name=BAS/> At the University of Sheffield, Kaiser set up a radar observatory to obtain radar measurements of the upper atmosphere on a local hillside (Onesmoor, near [[High Bradfield]]).<ref name=Times>{{cite news |title=Obituaries: Tom Kaiser |url=https://tomkaiser.tripod.com/times_obit.html |access-date=21 September 2024 |work=The Times |date=July 1998}}</ref><ref name=Hughes>{{cite web |last1=Hughes |first1=David |title=Tributes to Tom Kaiser, 1998 |url=https://tomkaiser.tripod.com/sheffield.html |publisher=University of Sheffield |access-date=23 September 2024}}</ref> Kaiser's other research interests included radar studies of the [[aurora]] and [[Whistler (radio)|Whistler]] wave studies.<ref name=BAS/>

Kaiser retired in 1987, and suffered from poor health in later years.<ref name=BAS/> In 1994 he received the [[Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society]] in [[geophysics]] for "his fundamental work and leadership in Space Geophysics."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Jordan |first1=C |title=Address of the President (Dr C. Jordan) on the Presentation of the Gold Medal to Professor T.R.Kaiser on Monday 1994, July 11. |url=https://tomkaiser.tripod.com/goldmedal.html |publisher=Royal Astronomical Society |access-date=23 September 2024}}</ref>

On 2 July 1998, Kaiser died in [[Palma de Majorca]], [[Spain]].<ref name=Independent/>

==Personal life==
Kaiser is the father of [[Nick Kaiser]], who has also been awarded the [[Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kaiser |first1=Nick |title=Thomas Reeve Kaiser 1924-1998 |url=https://tomkaiser.tripod.com/ |access-date=23 September 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Peacock |first1=John |title=Nick Kaiser Obituary |url=https://www.pressreader.com/usa/the-guardian-usa/20230811/282175065644336 |access-date=27 September 2024 |work=The Guardian USA |date=11 August 2023}}</ref>
